name: George Heriot's School Turrets
description: These conical corner turrets are part of George Heriot's School's main quadrangular building, begun in 1628 under master mason William Wallace and completed after his death in 1631. The turrets are a textbook example of a decorative feature that recurs across Edinburgh's grandest historic buildings - originally derived from defensive tower design on castles and tower houses, but adopted purely ornamentally on Renaissance-era civic and institutional buildings like this one to signal status and craftsmanship rather than to serve any defensive purpose. Heriot's own turrets carry ball-finialled lead roofs and, on the chapel turrets specifically, the carved arms of the school's founder, the royal goldsmith George Heriot.
interesting_fact: The same turret style appears on buildings all across the Old and New Town - from tenement stair-towers to grand institutions like this one - making it one of the most immediately recognisable architectural signatures of historic Edinburgh, quite apart from any single building it happens to sit on.

name: Ornate Iron Railings
description: These spear-topped cast-iron railings, fencing off a sunken basement stairwell on Keir Street, are one of the most common decorative features across Edinburgh's Georgian and Victorian streets. Cast iron became cheap and widely available in Scotland through the 18th and 19th centuries thanks to the country's ironworking industry, and virtually every New Town and tenement-lined Old Town street was fitted with railings like these - both to fence off the sunken 'area' in front of basement windows and doors, and simply to mark property boundaries in an attractive, uniform style. Most surviving examples, this one included, are on category-listed buildings and are protected as part of the character of Edinburgh's UNESCO World Heritage Site.
interesting_fact: During the Second World War, many of Edinburgh's railings were controversially requisitioned and melted down for the war effort - meaning surviving original ironwork like this, rather than post-war replacement railings, is now genuinely valued as a rarer historical survival.

name: Iron Boot Scraper
description: Set low into the stone stairs beside the railings at 18 Keir Street, this small cast-iron boot scraper is a fixture once found outside almost every Georgian and Victorian townhouse in Edinburgh. Before the city's streets were consistently paved and drained, mud, horse dung and general filth were unavoidable underfoot, and a boot scraper by the front door let residents and visitors clean their soles before stepping inside onto good carpets and floors. Most were cast in one piece with a flat blade for scraping and a small brush-holder or spike beside it, fixed directly into the stonework of the entrance steps - a small, functional detail now mostly obsolete but still visible outside thousands of Old and New Town doorways.
interesting_fact: Boot scrapers are one of the few genuinely functional (rather than purely decorative) pieces of historic street furniture still surviving in large numbers across Edinburgh, precisely because removing them meant chiselling them out of solid stone steps rather than simply unscrewing them.

name: Argyle House - 60s architectural eyesore
description: Argyle House is Edinburgh's most argued-about building - a hulking 1968 concrete-and-harling office block, designed by Michael Laird & Partners, that sits squarely across West Port in the middle of the Old Town's historic skyline. It went up on the site of John Croall & Son, a long-established garage and Rolls-Royce coachbuilder, after the developer Argyle Securities bought the land in 1961. Its route to approval ran through the city's 1953 Development Plan, which had rezoned the then-decaying West Port and High Riggs area for commercial use - quietly making land that had only ever supported housing suddenly valuable for large-scale office development. The Corporation Planning Committee approved the scheme in September 1966, in a decade when postwar modernisation was consistently prioritised over conservation concerns across British cities, Edinburgh included.
interesting_fact: Even architecture critics sympathetic to the building struggled to defend it - Colin McWilliam tried comparing its scale to Georgian terraces, but still admitted it was 'preposterously large and a potential rival to the Castle rock.' No public opposition to the scheme survives in the historical record, a telling contrast to how fiercely similar proposals are fought today.

name: Brown's Place
description: This quiet residential square opening off the Vennel takes its name from James Brown, who ran an inn next door in the Grassmarket. When the Flodden Wall - which had marked the edge of the city here since 1513 - was gradually demolished after 1815, following the Union and Napoleon's defeat removed any remaining need for city defences, Brown seized the chance to develop the land behind his inn, very likely reusing stone salvaged from the wall itself. By 1834 the square was being advertised as 'newly built.' It survived a serious threat in the 1960s, when numbers 1-3 stood derelict and the whole area was earmarked for demolition to expand the nearby art college - plans that were ultimately abandoned by decade's end, with those buildings rehabilitated in 1976.
interesting_fact: A residents' association formed in 1986 specifically to restore the square's shared garden, part of which had been concreted over at some point - reclaiming a small green space that Brown himself had built directly on top of the city's old defensive wall.

name: Stone Basements and Area Wells
description: The sunken stone-walled gap running beneath the railings at 16 Keir Street is a classic Edinburgh 'area' - a below-street-level space in front of a tenement's basement windows and door, built into virtually every Georgian and Victorian terrace in the city. Areas exist because these buildings' ground floors sit slightly raised above street level, with a basement or 'garden flat' beneath; rather than leaving that basement level buried and windowless, builders left a narrow open trench along the front wall, faced in dressed stone and fenced off with railings, so the basement rooms could get proper daylight and their own street-level door. The stone retaining wall and curving stair down to the basement door, visible here beneath the ironwork, are essentially unchanged from when the tenement was first built.
interesting_fact: Areas like this one are the reason Edinburgh's New Town and tenement streets needed so much cast ironwork in the first place - the railings weren't purely decorative, they were essential safety barriers stopping pedestrians from stepping straight down into a basement-level drop hidden right at the edge of the pavement.
